extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent practitioners evaluating computer-implemented inventions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for evaluating compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description, enablement, best mode, and related issues) particularized to computer-implemented inventions and functional claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory requirements for computer-implemented inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory requirements for computer-implemented inventions are the same as for all inventions, including subject matter eligibility and utility (35 U.S.C. 101), novelty (35 U.S.C. 102), nonobviousness (35 U.S.C. 103), definiteness (35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C.112, second paragraph), and the three separate and distinct requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C.112, first paragraph. Claims with computer-implemented functional limitations may invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 2106, 2107, 2161, 2181. Even if not construed under 112(f), functional language must be evaluated for written description and enablement under 112(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (35 U.S.C.112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to ensure claim scope does not overreach inventor’s contribution. This requirement is separate from enablement. Case law: Ariad, Reiffin, LizardTech, Rivera. See MPEP §§ 2162-2163.07(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus/species support for written description
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no special rule for supporting a genus by disclosure of a species; whether a genus is supported depends on the state of the art and the nature and breadth of the genus. Disclosure of species is sufficient if it conveys to one of ordinary skill that the inventor possessed the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the state of the art and whether disclosed species provide adequate support for claimed genus. See Hynix Semiconductor and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of generic or functional claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: Original claims that are generic or functional (or both) often fail written description because functional claims may claim a desired result without describing species that achieve that result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An adequate written description of a genus requires more than a generic statement of boundaries. Cases: Ariad, Enzo Biochem, Fiers, Eli Lilly. Examiners should scrutinize functional/genus claims for sufficient disclosure of species or structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to disclose algorithm/steps for computer-implemented functional claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For software-related functional claim limitations, the algorithm or steps/procedure for performing the computer function must be described with sufficient detail so that one of ordinary skill can understand how the inventor intended the function to be performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An algorithm may be expressed as a mathematical formula, in prose, as a flowchart, or in any manner that provides sufficient structure. It is not sufficient merely that one skilled in the art could write a program to achieve the function; the specification must explain how the inventor intends to achieve the function. See Finisar, Vasudevan; see MPEP §§ 2163.02 and 2181 IV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrelationship of hardware and software disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of sufficiency of disclosure for computer-implemented inventions requires inquiry into both disclosed hardware and disclosed software because of their interrelationship and interdependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical inquiry: does the disclosure reasonably convey to those skilled in the art that the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter as of the filing date. See Vasudevan Software v. MicroStrategy and Ariad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C.112(f)) corresponding structure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For means- (or step-) plus-function limitations under 112(f) or pre-AIA sixth paragraph, the specification must provide sufficient corresponding structure, materials, or acts that perform the entire claimed function; otherwise the applicant has failed to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (112(b) or pre-AIA second paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If insufficient corresponding structure is disclosed for a 112(f) limitation, make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) and also under 112(b). See In re Donaldson and MPEP § 2181 II.B.2(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification must disclose the best mode known to the inventor of practicing the invention at the time of filing; determination involves (1) a subjective inquiry whether inventor knew a best mode and (2) an objective inquiry whether that best mode was disclosed in sufficient detail to permit a person skilled in the art to practice it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only evidence of concealment (accidental or intentional) is relevant. For software, description of software functions normally satisfies best mode because writing code is within skill of the art; flow charts or source code listings are not required. Cases: In re Gay, Fonar, Spectra-Physics, Fonar Corp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C.112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All questions of enablement are evaluated against the claimed subject matter as a whole; focus on whether everything within the scope of the claim is enabled. See In re Wright, In re Wands, and MPEP §§ 2164-2164.08(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wands factors (factors for undue experimentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing undue experimentation, consider (1) breadth of the claims; (2) nature of the invention; (3) state of the prior art; (4) level of one of ordinary skill; (5) level of predictability in the art; (6) amount of direction provided by the inventor; (7) existence of working examples; and (8) quantity of experimentation needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The undue experimentation determination is a conclusion reached by weighing these factual considerations (In re Wands). Use them to justify an enablement rejection when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be commensurate with enablement (scope <= enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the claims must be less than or equal to the scope of the enablement provided by the specification; broad claim language chosen by the patentee is at the peril of losing claims that cannot be enabled across their full scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: Sitrick (claims covering movies and video games without enabling movies), MagSil (broad resistive-change claims not enabled across scope). Examiners should ensure specification enables the full scope claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's burden to establish reasonable basis before requiring rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO personnel must establish on the record a reasonable basis for questioning the adequacy of the disclosure to enable a person of ordinary skill without undue experimentation; once such basis is advanced, applicant must rebut and factually demonstrate sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Brown, In re Ghiron, In re Doyle, In re Scarbrough. Examiners should provide reasons and a prima facie case for lack of written description or enablement before completing office action. See MPEP §§ 2164 and 2163 guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claim language not invoking 112(f) is broadly construed
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is not limited to particular structure for performing a function and does not invoke 112(f), functional claim language is typically construed broadly to cover any and all embodiments that perform the recited function, raising concern whether disclosure enables the full scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because such claims encompass all devices/structures performing the function, ensure disclosure sufficiently enables the full scope; otherwise make enablement rejection. See In re Swinehart, AK Steel, In re Moore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification need not disclose well-known art but must enable novel aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification need not teach what is well known in the art; however, the applicant cannot rely on the knowledge of one skilled in the art to supply information required to enable the novel aspect of the claimed invention when that enabling knowledge is not in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: ALZA, Auto. Technologies, Genentech, Idenix. Use supplementation by known art cautiously; the novel aspects must be enabled in the specification itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description may be satisfied by originally-filed claims or other portions
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory written description may be found in originally-filed claims or any other portion of the originally-filed specification, but that does not mean all originally-filed claims have adequate written support; the specification must be examined to assess support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Koller, In re Gardner, In re Wertheim. Examiners must verify that originally-filed material indeed conveys possession of claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to show possession for written description
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by describing the claimed invention with all limitations using words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, actual reduction to practice, disclosure showing invention was 'ready for patenting', distinguishing identifying characteristics, or, for biological materials, an appropriate deposit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and cases: Lockwood, Pfaff, Eli Lilly, Amgen, Enzo Biochem. For biological deposits follow 37 CFR 1.801 et seq.; deposit is not a substitute for a written description and written description of deposited material should be as complete as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections for lack of written description or enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C.112(a) (written description) or 35 U.S.C.112(a) (enablement) must be made when the specification does not provide adequate disclosure to demonstrate possession or to enable the full scope of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should establish a prima facie case, conduct thorough prior art review and examination on merits for other statutory requirements prior to completing an office action that includes such a rejection. See MPEP §§ 2163, 2164, 2181.
